chapter.title: Sorting
chapter.summary: How computers put things in order: the simple sorts, the fast divide-and-conquer sorts, the linear-time sorts and how to use sorting to solve problems.

lessons.title: Sorting basics: bubble, selection, insertion
lessons.summary: The three simple O(n²) sorts, what stability and in-place mean, and why insertion sort still matters inside real library sorts.

parts.label: Concept
parts.body:
## Why learn sorting at all?

Almost nobody writes their own sort in production: every language ships a good one. You learn sorting for three reasons:

1. **It is the cleanest place to learn algorithm analysis.** Comparing two sorts teaches you how to reason about time, space, stability and best/worst cases.
2. **Many problems become easy once the data is sorted.** Two pointers, binary search, merging intervals, greedy choices and duplicate detection all start with "sort first".
3. **Interviewers ask about it.** "Which sort would you use here, and why?" is a common follow-up.

## The vocabulary

- **Comparison sort**: decides order only by comparing two items (`a < b`). There is a proven lower bound: any comparison sort needs **Ω(n log n)** comparisons in the worst case.
- **In-place**: uses `O(1)` extra memory (a few variables), not a second array.
- **Stable**: items that compare equal keep their original relative order. If you sort people by age and two people are both 30, a stable sort keeps them in the order they had before. This matters when you sort by one field, then another (sort by name, then stably by age: ties on age stay alphabetical).
- **Adaptive**: runs faster when the input is already nearly sorted.

## Bubble sort

Repeatedly walk the array; swap any adjacent pair that is out of order. After pass 1 the **largest** element has "bubbled" to the end; after pass 2 the second largest is in place, and so on.

Add an early exit: if a full pass makes **no swap**, the array is sorted, so stop. With that flag, bubble sort is `O(n)` on already-sorted input.

## Selection sort

Split the array into a sorted prefix and an unsorted rest. On each step, **select the minimum** of the rest and swap it to the front of the unsorted part.

- Always `O(n²)` comparisons, even if sorted (it cannot tell).
- Only `O(n)` swaps, the fewest of the three. Useful when writes are expensive (flash memory).
- **Not stable** with the usual swap: swapping the minimum over a far element can jump an equal item past another equal item.

## Insertion sort

This is how most people sort a hand of playing cards. Keep a sorted prefix. Take the next element (the **key**) and slide it left past every larger element until it fits.

- Best case `O(n)` (already sorted: each key needs one comparison).
- Worst case `O(n²)` (reverse sorted).
- **Stable**, in-place and adaptive. For small arrays (about 10 to 50 items) it is the **fastest** practical sort, because it has tiny constants and good cache behaviour. That is why real sorts (Timsort in Python and Java, introsort in C++) switch to insertion sort for small pieces.

## Worked example: insertion sort on `[5, 2, 4, 1]`

| step | key | array after inserting key | work |
|---|---|---|---|
| start | | `[5]` sorted, `[2, 4, 1]` not yet | sorted prefix is `[5]` |
| 1 | 2 | `[2, 5]` then `[4, 1]` | shift 5 right, place 2 |
| 2 | 4 | `[2, 4, 5]` then `[1]` | shift 5, place 4 |
| 3 | 1 | `[1, 2, 4, 5]` | shift 5, 4, 2, place 1 |

## Choosing between them

| | bubble | selection | insertion |
|---|---|---|---|
| best | O(n) with flag | O(n²) | **O(n)** |
| worst | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(n²) |
| swaps/writes | many | **O(n)** | many shifts |
| stable | yes | no | **yes** |
| use | teaching | few writes | small or nearly sorted data |

## What the built-in sort does

- **JavaScript** `arr.sort()` without a comparator sorts **as strings**: `[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 9]`. Always pass `(a, b) => a - b` for numbers. Modern engines guarantee stability.
- **Python** `sorted()` / `list.sort()` use **Timsort**: stable, `O(n log n)` worst case, `O(n)` on nearly sorted data. `key=` is evaluated once per item.
- **Java** sorts primitives with dual-pivot quicksort (not stable) and objects with Timsort (stable).
- **C++** `std::sort` is introsort (not stable); use `std::stable_sort` when ties matter.

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting the early-exit flag in bubble sort, then claiming it is adaptive.
- Writing a numeric comparator as `a > b` returning a boolean in JS. It must return a **number** (negative, zero, positive).
- Assuming a sort is stable when it is not.

code.source:
def insertion_sort(a):
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        key = a[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and a[j] > key:   # strict > keeps it stable
            a[j + 1] = a[j]
            j -= 1
        a[j + 1] = key
    return a

def selection_sort(a):
    for i in range(len(a) - 1):
        m = min(range(i, len(a)), key=a.__getitem__)
        a[i], a[m] = a[m], a[i]
    return a

parts.label: Hand-tracing
parts.body:
## Trace insertion sort on `[3, 1, 4, 1, 5]`

Hand-tracing is the skill that catches off-by-one bugs, and interviewers love to ask for it. Track the array after each outer iteration; the part in square brackets is the sorted prefix.

| i | key | comparisons / shifts | array |
|---|---|---|---|
| start | | | `[3] 1 4 1 5` |
| 1 | 1 | 3 > 1: shift 3 | `[1 3] 4 1 5` |
| 2 | 4 | 3 > 4? no, stop | `[1 3 4] 1 5` |
| 3 | 1 | 4 > 1 shift, 3 > 1 shift, 1 > 1? **no** stop | `[1 1 3 4] 5` |
| 4 | 5 | 4 > 5? no | `1 1 3 4 5` |

Notice step 3: the comparison `a[j] > key` is **strict**, so the new 1 stops right after the old 1. The two equal 1s keep their original order, which is what makes insertion sort stable. Changing `>` to `>=` would still sort, but it would swap equal items and lose stability (and do extra work).

## Count the work

For input of size `n`:

- **Comparisons** in the worst case (reverse sorted): `1 + 2 + ... + (n-1) = n(n-1)/2`. For `n = 1000` that is 499,500.
- **Best case**: `n - 1` comparisons, no shifts.
- The number of shifts equals the number of **inversions** (pairs `i < j` with `a[i] > a[j]`). That is why insertion sort is fast on nearly sorted data: few inversions means little work. The running time is `O(n + inversions)`.

## Stability in practice

Suppose records `(Asha, 30), (Bo, 25), (Cy, 30)` are sorted by name. Now sort by age with a **stable** sort: `Bo 25, Asha 30, Cy 30`. Ties on age stay alphabetical, so you get "by age, then name" for free. With an unstable sort the 30s might come out as `Cy, Asha`. When a task says "break ties by original order", you need a stable sort or an explicit index in the key.

## Choosing under constraints

| constraint | pick |
|---|---|
| fewest writes (flash memory, expensive swaps) | selection sort |
| nearly sorted input | insertion sort |
| must be stable and simple | insertion sort |
| tiny array inside a bigger algorithm | insertion sort |
| anything large | library sort, `O(n log n)` |

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

Sorting questions are rarely "implement bubble sort". They test whether you can **compare algorithms on several axes** (time, space, stability, adaptivity) and whether you know when sorting is the lever that turns a quadratic solution into `O(n log n)`.

## Questions with model answers

### 1. What does "stable" mean and when does it matter?

**Model answer.** A stable sort keeps equal items in their original relative order. It matters when you sort records by multiple keys in passes (sort by name, then stably by age), when the display order has meaning (a table you re-sort by clicking column headers), and inside radix sort where each digit pass must preserve the previous one. Insertion sort, merge sort, Timsort and counting sort (right-to-left) are stable; selection sort, heap sort and typical quick sort are not.

### 2. Why is insertion sort used inside Timsort and introsort even though it is O(n²)?

**Model answer.** Big-O hides constants. On tiny arrays (roughly under 32 to 64 items) insertion sort has almost no overhead, no recursion, and sequential memory access, so it beats the asymptotically better sorts. Timsort also detects naturally ordered "runs" and extends short runs with insertion sort before merging them. So the fast sorts split big inputs until the pieces are small enough that insertion sort wins.

### 3. Compare bubble, selection and insertion sort. Which would you pick?

**Model answer.** All are `O(n²)` worst case and `O(1)` space. Bubble sort is only a teaching tool. Selection sort does the fewest writes (`O(n)` swaps) but is not stable and always `O(n²)`. Insertion sort is stable, adaptive (`O(n)` on nearly sorted data) and has the best constants. If I must pick one of the three, it is insertion sort; in production I use the library sort.

### 4. Why can't a comparison sort beat n log n?

**Model answer.** A comparison sort is a binary decision tree: each comparison has two outcomes, and the tree must have a leaf for every one of the `n!` possible orderings. A binary tree with `n!` leaves has height at least `log₂(n!)`, which is `Θ(n log n)` by Stirling's approximation. So the worst case needs at least that many comparisons. Counting and radix sort escape the bound by using the key's value, not comparisons.

### 5. How would you sort a file too large for memory?

**Model answer.** External merge sort. Read chunks that fit in memory, sort each chunk (quick sort) and write it to disk as a sorted run. Then do a k-way merge of the runs using a min-heap holding the front item of each run, streaming output to disk. Total `O(n log n)` with sequential I/O, which is what disks are good at.

### 6. A teammate wrote `arr.sort((a, b) => a > b)` in JavaScript. What is wrong?

**Model answer.** The comparator must return a negative, zero or positive **number**. A boolean converts to 1 or 0, so it never returns a negative value and "a before b" is never signalled; results are engine-dependent and wrong. The fix is `(a, b) => a - b` (safe for normal numbers) or `a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0`.

## Rapid-fire

- **Fastest sort for 10⁶ integers between 0 and 1000?** Counting sort, `O(n + k)`.
- **Sort a linked list?** Merge sort, `O(n log n)`, `O(1)` extra space with the bottom-up version.
- **Is `Arrays.sort(int[])` stable?** Irrelevant for primitives (equal ints are indistinguishable); objects use a stable Timsort.
- **Nearly sorted data?** Insertion sort or Timsort.
- **Need the median only?** Quickselect, `O(n)` average.

keyPoints: Comparison sorts cannot beat Ω(n log n) in the worst case; the three simple sorts are O(n²).
Stable means equal items keep their original order; it matters when you sort by several fields in turn.
Insertion sort is stable, adaptive and the best of the simple sorts: O(n) on nearly sorted data.
Selection sort does the fewest swaps (O(n)) but is not stable and never gets faster.
Real library sorts use insertion sort on small chunks. In JS always pass a numeric comparator.

With no comparator JS converts items to strings and compares them, so "1" < "10" < "9". Pass (a, b) => a - b for numeric order.

options: It cannot detect order, so it still does about n²/2 comparisons

check.why: Selection sort always scans the whole unsorted rest to find the minimum, so it performs the same comparisons regardless of input order.

lessons.title: Merge sort, quick sort and quickselect
lessons.summary: Divide and conquer sorting in O(n log n): how merge sort and quick sort split work, the partition step, pivot choice, and quickselect for the kth element.

parts.label: Concept
parts.body:
## Divide and conquer

The simple sorts fix one element per pass, which is why they cost `O(n²)`. The fast sorts **split the problem in half** and solve each half separately. Splitting a problem of size `n` in half repeatedly takes `log₂ n` levels, and each level does `O(n)` total work, giving `O(n log n)`. For `n = 1,000,000` that is about 20 million steps instead of 1 trillion.

## Merge sort: split first, work later

1. **Split** the array into two halves.
2. **Recursively sort** each half (an array of 0 or 1 items is already sorted: the base case).
3. **Merge** the two sorted halves into one sorted array.

All the real work is the **merge**. With two sorted lists and a pointer at the front of each, repeatedly take the smaller front item. Each item is moved once, so merging `n` items costs `O(n)`.

Properties:

- `O(n log n)` in **every** case (best, average, worst). Predictable.
- **Stable** if you take from the left half when items are equal (`<=`).
- Needs `O(n)` extra space for the merge buffer.
- Great for **linked lists** (merge needs no extra space and no random access) and for **external sorting** (data bigger than memory, merged from disk).
- Counting **inversions** (pairs out of order) is a classic add-on: while merging, each time you take from the right half, every item left in the left half forms an inversion with it.

## Quick sort: work first, split later

1. **Choose a pivot**.
2. **Partition**: rearrange so everything `< pivot` is on the left and everything `>= pivot` on the right. The pivot is now in its **final sorted position**.
3. Recursively quick sort the left and right parts.

There is no merge step: partitioning does the work in place.

### Lomuto partition (simple)

Use the last item as pivot. Keep an index `i` marking the end of the "smaller" zone. Scan with `j`; whenever `a[j] < pivot`, grow the zone and swap `a[j]` into it. Finally swap the pivot into position `i`.

### Pivot choice is everything

- Pivot is always the smallest or largest (for example, last item of an already-sorted array): one side is empty, depth is `n`, total `O(n²)`.
- Pivot near the median: balanced, `O(n log n)`.
- Fixes: **random pivot** (expected `O(n log n)` for every input), **median of three** (first, middle, last), or the **three-way partition** (`<`, `==`, `>`) which makes arrays full of duplicates `O(n)`.

Properties: average `O(n log n)`, worst `O(n²)`, in-place (`O(log n)` stack on average), **not stable**. In practice it is usually the fastest comparison sort because it is cache friendly and has tiny constants.

## Merge sort vs quick sort

| | merge sort | quick sort |
|---|---|---|
| worst case | **O(n log n)** | O(n²) (unlucky pivots) |
| extra space | O(n) | O(log n) |
| stable | **yes** | no |
| best for | linked lists, stability, external data | arrays in memory, speed |

## Quickselect: kth smallest without full sort

If you only need the **kth smallest** element, you don't need everything sorted. After partitioning, the pivot sits at index `p`:

- `p == k`: done, the pivot is the answer.
- `p > k`: the answer is in the left part only.
- `p < k`: the answer is in the right part only.

You recurse into **one** side, so the expected work is `n + n/2 + n/4 + ... = O(n)`. Worst case is `O(n²)` (fixed with a random pivot, or median-of-medians for a guaranteed `O(n)`). This is the engine behind "Kth Largest Element in an Array" (the alternative is a heap, `O(n log k)`).

## Worked example: merging `[1, 4, 7]` and `[2, 3, 9]`

| left ptr | right ptr | compare | output so far |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2 | 1 ≤ 2 → take 1 | `[1]` |
| 4 | 2 | 2 < 4 → take 2 | `[1, 2]` |
| 4 | 3 | 3 < 4 → take 3 | `[1, 2, 3]` |
| 4 | 9 | 4 ≤ 9 → take 4 | `[1, 2, 3, 4]` |
| 7 | 9 | take 7 | `[1, 2, 3, 4, 7]` |
| (left empty) | 9 | append rest | `[1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 9]` |

## Common mistakes

- Using `<` instead of `<=` when merging, which makes merge sort **unstable**.
- Choosing the first or last element as pivot on possibly-sorted input.
- Recursing into **both** sides in quickselect (turns `O(n)` into `O(n log n)`).
- Off-by-one on the middle index; use `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2` to avoid integer overflow in Java and C++.

code.source:
import random

def merge_sort(a):
    if len(a) <= 1:
        return a
    mid = len(a) // 2
    left, right = merge_sort(a[:mid]), merge_sort(a[mid:])
    out, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:        # <= keeps it stable
            out.append(left[i]); i += 1
        else:
            out.append(right[j]); j += 1
    return out + left[i:] + right[j:]

def quickselect(a, k):                 # kth smallest, 0-based
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        r = random.randint(lo, hi)
        a[r], a[hi] = a[hi], a[r]
        i = lo
        for j in range(lo, hi):
            if a[j] < a[hi]:
                a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]; i += 1
        a[i], a[hi] = a[hi], a[i]
        if i == k: return a[i]
        if i < k: lo = i + 1
        else: hi = i - 1

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

Divide-and-conquer sorting questions check that you can **explain the mechanism** (not just name it), analyse best and worst cases, and pick the right algorithm for the data structure and constraints at hand.

## Questions with model answers

### 1. Explain quick sort and its worst case.

**Model answer.** Pick a pivot, partition the array so smaller items are on its left and larger on its right (the pivot lands in its final position), then recurse on both sides. When pivots split roughly evenly the depth is `log n` and each level costs `O(n)`, so `O(n log n)`. If the pivot is always the minimum or maximum, one side is empty, the depth is `n`, and the cost is `O(n²)`. This happens with a fixed first or last pivot on sorted input. A random pivot makes the bad case astronomically unlikely, and a three-way partition handles many duplicates.

### 2. Why is quick sort usually faster than merge sort in practice, despite the worse worst case?

**Model answer.** Quick sort works in place on contiguous memory, so it is cache friendly, and its inner loop is a tight compare-and-swap with small constants. Merge sort copies data to and from a buffer, which costs memory bandwidth and allocation. Production sorts like introsort get both: quick sort for speed, switching to heap sort if the recursion depth grows too large, which caps the worst case at `O(n log n)`.

### 3. When would you choose merge sort over quick sort?

**Model answer.** When I need stability, a guaranteed `O(n log n)`, or when the data is a **linked list** (merging needs no random access and no extra space) or too large for memory (external sort merges sorted runs from disk). Also when sorting objects where equal-key order must be preserved.

### 4. How do you find the kth largest element? Compare the options.

**Model answer.** Sorting is `O(n log n)`. A min-heap of size `k` is `O(n log k)` and works on a stream because it only ever stores `k` items. Quickselect partitions around a pivot and recurses into only the side containing the target index, giving `O(n)` on average and `O(n²)` in the worst case (mitigated with a random pivot, or median-of-medians for a guaranteed `O(n)` at a high constant). For an interview I mention all three, then pick the heap for streams and quickselect for a static array.

### 5. How would you count inversions in an array in O(n log n)?

**Model answer.** Run merge sort and count during the merge. When the next item taken comes from the right half, it is smaller than every item still waiting in the left half, so add `leftRemaining` to the count. Inversions inside each half are counted by the recursive calls. The total is the sum. A brute force check of every pair is `O(n²)`.

### 6. What is the recursion depth risk in quick sort and how do you reduce it?

**Model answer.** With bad pivots the depth reaches `n`, which can overflow the call stack. The standard fix is to recurse into the **smaller** partition and loop on the larger one; that bounds the stack at `O(log n)` regardless of pivot luck.

## Rapid-fire

- **Merge sort extra space?** `O(n)` for arrays, `O(log n)` stack for linked lists.
- **Is quick sort stable?** No (partitioning swaps distant items).
- **Which is best for a linked list?** Merge sort.
- **Time to merge two sorted lists of sizes m and n?** `O(m + n)`.
- **Why `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2`?** Avoids integer overflow of `lo + hi`.

complexity.time: O(n log n) avg, O(n²) worst

keyPoints: Divide and conquer turns n² into n log n: log n levels of halving, O(n) work per level.
Merge sort does the work in the merge step: guaranteed O(n log n), stable, O(n) space, ideal for linked lists.
Quick sort does the work in the partition step: in place, fastest in practice, but O(n²) with bad pivots, so randomise.
After a partition the pivot is in its final sorted position; that fact powers quickselect.
Quickselect recurses into one side only, finding the kth element in expected O(n).

Each partition puts every other element on one side, so recursion depth is n
The pivot is compared with itself

check.why: The pivot is the maximum, so one side has n-1 items and the other is empty. Depth n with O(n) work per level gives O(n²).

options: It recurses into only one side of the partition
check.q: What makes quickselect O(n) on average instead of O(n log n)?
check.why: The work shrinks geometrically: n + n/2 + n/4 + ... ≈ 2n, because one side is discarded each round.

options: It has O(n log n) worst-case time and is stable

check.why: Merge sort never degrades and keeps equal items in order when merging with <=; quick sort can hit O(n²) and is not stable.

lessons.title: Counting sort, radix sort and sorting patterns
lessons.summary: Linear-time sorts that avoid comparisons, plus the interview patterns built on sorting: custom comparators, sort-then-scan, and sort-by-key.

parts.label: Concept
parts.body:
## Beating n log n

The `Ω(n log n)` bound applies only to **comparison** sorts. If the keys are small integers, you can sort without comparing at all.

## Counting sort

Use when keys are integers in a known small range `0..k`.

1. Make an array `count[0..k]` and count how many times each value appears.
2. Convert counts to **prefix sums**: `count[v]` becomes the number of items `<= v`, i.e. where the last copy of `v` ends.
3. Walk the input **from the right**, put each item at `count[v] - 1` and decrement. Walking right-to-left keeps it **stable**.

Cost `O(n + k)` time and space. It is excellent when `k` is about the size of `n` (ages, exam marks, letters) and terrible when `k` is huge (sorting 10 numbers up to 10⁹).

The simplified version (rebuild the array by writing `v` exactly `count[v]` times) is fine for plain integers but loses stability for records, so it cannot serve as the pass inside radix sort.

## Radix sort

Sort numbers **digit by digit**, from the least significant digit (LSD) to the most significant, using a **stable** sort (counting sort) for each digit.

Why does it work? After sorting by the last digit, then stably by the tens digit, items are ordered by (tens, ones). Each later pass keeps the earlier order among ties, so after the final pass they are ordered by the full number.

Cost `O(d · (n + b))` for `d` digits in base `b`. For 32-bit integers with base 256 that is 4 passes: effectively linear.

## Bucket sort

Spread values into `m` buckets by range (for uniformly distributed floats in `[0, 1)`, bucket `i` holds values in `[i/m, (i+1)/m)`), sort each small bucket (insertion sort), then concatenate. Expected `O(n)` for uniform data, `O(n²)` if everything lands in one bucket.

This idea also solves **Top K Frequent Elements** in `O(n)`: make buckets indexed by frequency (a value can appear at most `n` times), then read buckets from high to low.

## Sorting as a problem-solving tool

Whenever a problem says "pairs", "closest", "overlap", "duplicates" or "order", ask: *would this be easier sorted?* Sorting costs `O(n log n)` once, and then a single `O(n)` scan finishes the job.

1. **Sort, then two pointers.** 3Sum, closest pair, container problems.
2. **Sort, then merge neighbours.** Merge Intervals: sort by start, then extend the current interval while the next start is `<=` its end.
3. **Sort, then greedy.** Meeting rooms, assign cookies, boats to save people.
4. **Sort by a custom key.** Largest Number (compare `a+b` vs `b+a` as strings), Custom Sort String (rank by position in the order string).
5. **Sort to detect duplicates or group.** Sorted letters are a canonical key for anagrams.

## Writing a comparator correctly

A comparator answers "should `a` come before `b`?" with a negative number (before), zero (tie) or positive (after).

- **Never** return `a - b` for values that can overflow (Java `int`). Use `Integer.compare(a, b)`.
- A comparator must be **consistent** (transitive); inconsistent ones can crash or loop in some sorts.
- To sort by several fields, compare the first; only if tied compare the second. In Python use a tuple key: `key=lambda p: (-p.score, p.name)`.

## Worked example: counting sort of `[4, 2, 2, 8, 3, 3, 1]`

| step | state |
|---|---|
| count (indices 0..8) | `[0,1,2,2,1,0,0,0,1]` |
| prefix sums | `[0,1,3,5,6,6,6,6,7]` |
| place 1 | goes to index 0 |
| place 3 (rightmost first) | goes to index 4 |
| place 3 (next) | goes to index 3 |
| result | `[1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 8]` |

## How to pick a sort in an interview

- Small input or nearly sorted: insertion sort / the built-in.
- General case in memory: the built-in sort; mention `O(n log n)`.
- Stability needed: merge sort / Timsort.
- Keys are small integers: counting or radix sort, `O(n)`.
- Only the top k or kth: heap `O(n log k)` or quickselect `O(n)`.
- Huge data on disk: external merge sort.

code.source:
def counting_sort(a, k):
    count = [0] * (k + 1)
    for v in a:
        count[v] += 1
    for v in range(1, k + 1):
        count[v] += count[v - 1]
    out = [0] * len(a)
    for v in reversed(a):             # right to left = stable
        count[v] -= 1
        out[count[v]] = v
    return out

# Sort by several fields: highest score first, then name
people.sort(key=lambda p: (-p["score"], p["name"]))

# Largest Number: order by which concatenation is bigger
from functools import cmp_to_key
def largest_number(nums):
    s = sorted(map(str, nums), key=cmp_to_key(lambda a, b: -1 if a + b > b + a else 1))
    return "0" if s[0] == "0" else "".join(s)

parts.label: Worked problems
parts.body:
## Problem 1: Sort Colors (Dutch national flag)

**Task.** An array holds only 0, 1 and 2. Sort it in place in one pass without using the library sort.

**Why not counting sort?** It works (two passes, `O(n)`), but the follow-up is always "can you do it in **one** pass with `O(1)` space?". The answer is a three-way partition.

**Idea.** Keep three zones: `[0, low)` are all 0s, `[low, mid)` are all 1s, `(high, end]` are all 2s. The unknown zone is `[mid, high]`. Look at `a[mid]`:

- `0`: swap with `a[low]`, then `low++`, `mid++`.
- `1`: already in the right zone, `mid++`.
- `2`: swap with `a[high]`, then `high--` (**do not** advance `mid`: the swapped-in value is unexamined).

| a | low | mid | high | action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `[2,0,1]` | 0 | 0 | 2 | a[mid]=2, swap with a[2] → `[1,0,2]`, high=1 |
| `[1,0,2]` | 0 | 0 | 1 | a[mid]=1, mid=1 |
| `[1,0,2]` | 0 | 1 | 1 | a[mid]=0, swap with a[0] → `[0,1,2]`, low=1, mid=2 |
| done | | 2 > high | | `[0,1,2]` |

`O(n)` time, `O(1)` space, one pass. This is exactly the three-way partition that makes quick sort fast on arrays full of duplicates.

## Problem 2: Merge Intervals

**Task.** Merge all overlapping intervals: `[[1,3],[8,10],[2,6],[15,18]]` → `[[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]`.

**Idea.** Sort by **start**. Then one scan: keep the last merged interval; if the next interval starts at or before its end, extend the end with `max(end, next.end)`; otherwise start a new one.

Why sorting is the key: once sorted by start, any interval that overlaps the current group must be the next one. Without sorting you would compare every pair, `O(n²)`.

**Complexity.** `O(n log n)` for the sort, `O(n)` scan. **Pitfall:** use `max` for the end. `[1,10]` followed by `[2,3]` must stay `[1,10]`.

## Problem 3: Kth Largest Element

Three valid answers, and an interviewer expects you to compare them:

| approach | time | space | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sort and index | `O(n log n)` | `O(1)`/`O(n)` | simplest, fine for small inputs |
| Min-heap of size k | `O(n log k)` | `O(k)` | works on streams, stable performance |
| Quickselect | `O(n)` average | `O(1)` | modifies the array, `O(n²)` worst without random pivot |

Say which you would ship: for a **stream** or when `k` is small, the heap; for a one-shot array where mutation is fine, quickselect.

## Problem 4: Sort an almost sorted array

**Task.** Each element is at most `k` positions from its sorted position.

**Idea.** A min-heap of size `k + 1`. Push the first `k + 1` items; repeatedly pop the minimum (it must be the next output, because the true minimum of the remaining items lies within the next `k + 1`) and push the next item. `O(n log k)`, which beats `O(n log n)` when `k` is small. Mention insertion sort as the `O(nk)` alternative.

keyPoints: The n log n bound only applies to comparison sorts; integer keys in a small range can be sorted in O(n + k).
Counting sort counts, takes prefix sums, then places items from right to left so it stays stable.
Radix sort applies a stable sort digit by digit, least significant first.
Many problems become easy after one O(n log n) sort followed by an O(n) scan: sort first, then two pointers, merge or greedy.
A comparator returns negative, zero or positive; use tuple keys or compare helpers instead of risky subtraction.

To avoid the prefix sum step
check.q: Why does counting sort place items while walking the input from right to left?
check.why: With prefix sums marking the end of each key's range, filling from the right puts the last equal item last, preserving original order. Radix sort depends on this.

options: Sorting exam marks from 0 to 100 for a million students
Sorting 20 numbers that can be as large as 10⁹
check.q: When is counting sort a bad choice?
check.why: Its cost is O(n + k) and it allocates k counters. With k = 10⁹ and n = 20, the range dominates and wastes time and memory.

check.q: In LSD radix sort, why must each digit pass use a stable sort?
check.why: After sorting by the tens digit, items with equal tens must stay ordered by their ones digit. A non-stable pass would scramble that order and give a wrong result.
